item.title: Once-hot AI trade leaves Korean stocks struggling for buyers
item.description: South Korea's stock market is facing a significant downturn after a dominant run in the global AI sector, as the Kospi has dropped 22% since its peak, marking it as the worst performer in the second half of the year. A startling 70% decline in turnover has prompted withdrawals from both foreign and local investors.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: South Korea spent much of this year as a poster child of the scorching global AI trade. Now, by almost every measure, the $4.3 trillion stock market is rapidly losing relevance with investors.Turnover has collapsed 70% from its peak in late May, foreigners are retreating at the fastest pace in Asia and local retail investors are also pulling back. The Kospi, the world's best-performing equities benchmark in the first half, has since lost 22% to be the worst in the second half while its AI-heavy Taiwanese and US peers set new highs.Behind the reversal is a market whose AI fortunes hinge disproportionately on Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc, the two memory-chip giants at the heart of the global AI supply chain. That concentration is now a liability as investors question the durability of memory chips' boom cycle, while the leverage-driven selloff in the past has made some global funds hesitant to return.Read more: Wall Street Week Ahead: Bank earnings, CPI headline busy markets week as S&P 500 hovers near recordsSkepticism over memory chip demand was on full display when shares of Samsung fell on Thursday despite surge in quarterly profit.Korea is now struggling to lure buyers, a problem amplified by the nearing completion of combined 55 trillion won ($41 billion) stock buybacks by Samsung and SK Hynix. Repurchases by the two chipmakers accounted for the bulk of the $23 billion worth of buy orders in the market last month, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co. We have seen capital increasingly gravitate back toward US equities, contributing to ongoing foreign outflows from the Korean market, said Richard Tang, head of research Hong Kong at Julius Baer.Read more: ET Alpha Wealth Summit 2.0: What do Shah Rukh Khan and SIFs have in common? Radhika Gupta explainsIndividual investors, a key force behind Kospi's 100% rally in the first half, remain elusive following the July rout.Margin loans outstanding have hovered around 33 trillion won over the past month, after peaking at 38.6 trillion won in June, according to data from the Korea Financial Investment Association.

item.title: Global Market Today: Asian shares cautious as earnings loom, oil slips
item.description: Trade was thin with Japan markets shut and the US on a partial holiday ahead of the earnings season with major US banks kicking off on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: SYDNEY: Asian share markets got off to a cautious start on Monday as earnings season loomed as a challenge to sky-high tech valuations, while oil was choppy after strikes on shipping and airports in the Gulf.There was considerable confusion about President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, which neither side had confirmed.Read more: Nifty Outlook: Can bulls sustain recovery after 8-week losing streak?Trump's proposal for Russia to increase its exports of diesel was also under fire from Republican and Democratic senators as potentially illegal.Brent futures started higher but soon slipped 1.1% to $103.50 a barrel, away from the recent top of $109.97, while US crude futures lost 1.2% to $90.73 a barrel.South Korean stocks fell 1.1%, while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was little changed.On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures edged up 0.2%, while Nasdaq futures firmed 0.5%. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures firmed 0.4%, while DAX futures gained 0.4% and FTSE futures added 0.3%.Trade was thin with Japan markets shut and the US on a partial holiday ahead of the earnings season with major US banks kicking off on Tuesday.S&P 500 earnings are expected to have jumped by more than 30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, though the bulk of that comes from the tech sector.My Bui, an economist at AMP, noted all the gains in the S&P 500 since mid-September had been in tech, while investors were demanding higher yields to fund the massive borrowing for AI.The US investment-grade credit default swap index, which tracks the cost of insurance against default, had also risen sharply to its highest level since the Iran war began. Overall, wider spreads suggest investors are questioning whether AI revenues can keep pace with rising borrowing costs, added Bui. Corporate bond issuance to fund AI capex, combined with wider high-yield spreads, will raise refinancing costs as the current wave of debt matures over the next few years. US CPI TO HEAT UP, BUT CORE COOLERThe flood of corporate debt has added to pressure in sovereign markets, driving Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week and lifting the discount applied to company earnings.The market faces fresh challenges this week from US data on consumer and producer prices and retail sales. Rising energy costs are expected to lift CPI by a hefty 0.6% to an annual 3.7%, though the core is seen cooler at 0.2% and 2.5%. Oil prices remain higher than we had assumed as shipping costs have soared, and product prices are even higher, said Bruce Kasman, head of global economics at JPMorgan. The signals on inflation point to a sharp rebound in headline inflation that will squeeze purchasing power and a firming in core inflation that will keep central banks focused on near-term hikes. Markets imply only an 18% chance of a rate rise from the Federal Reserve this month, but an 85% chance of a hike in December. Investors are also wagering on hikes in the EU, Japan and UK before year end.In currency markets, the euro remained on the defensive at $1.1201 having fallen for five weeks straight amid concerns about government deficits in Europe.The dollar index held near 17-month highs at 102.25, but has stalled on the yen at 158.15 as the threat of Japanese intervention deters speculators for now.In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold rose 0.3% to $4,206 an ounce, having managed to bounce more than 1% last week.
